description: Solo team - not looking for additional members.
summary: Mission Design Lab is a free browser game in which 1–4 players design, manage and fly a complete space mission, from the first science question to the end of operations. Players choose mission objectives first; the objectives unlock only the instruments that can serve them. They then pick an orbit, launch vehicle, power, communications, ground segment and spacecraft bus, while live budgets for mass, power, data, cost, schedule and risk show every trade-off: add a radar, and the power, link margin and budget turn red. The team signs off, the mission is launched and simulated month by month, and the spacecraft reports what the design did to it. A final report scores the design, compares it with a real NASA mission of the same kind, and a Mishap Board mode lets players work backwards from a failed mission to the decision that lost it. The steps follow NASA's six-stage science mission process, JPL Concept Maturity Levels and Goddard Mission Design Lab study levels. It makes the abstract trade-offs of mission design something students can try, break and fix in one session, with no install.
details:
What it does

Mission Design Lab is a browser game that lets 1–4 players take a space mission from a science question to the end of operations. It runs on any computer, Chromebook or tablet with a web browser, with nothing to install: https://vcdwio.github.io/CDSpace/

Players work through eight steps, grouped by the six stages of NASA's science mission process (need and goals, concept, requirements, design, build and verify, implement):

  • Brief: choose a scenario (CubeSat Starter, Earth Watch, Space Telescope, Lunar Explorer, Red Planet, Outer Planets, or the speculative Deep Space Express) and the study level (Office Hours, Concept Development, Trade Study or Point Design).
  • Objectives first: the science goals unlock only the instruments that can serve them.
  • Design all four segments: launch (launch vehicle and trajectory), space (instruments, bus, power, propulsion, attitude control, data handling), ground (stations and link) and users (operations and data delivery).
  • Live budgets: mass, power, data volume, link margin, Δv, cost, schedule and risk update on every click and turn red when a limit is broken. A Concept Maturity Level meter rises as the design closes.
  • Team review: up to four players share the roles of Mission Planner, Spacecraft Engineer, Science Lead and Comms & Resources, each with a personal goal, and everyone signs before launch.
  • Fly it: a seeded month-by-month simulation with launch, eclipse, radiation, degradation and random failures. The spacecraft itself reports what the design did to it.
  • Report: a score, a newspaper-style front page, and a side-by-side comparison with a real NASA mission of the same kind (for example Landsat 9, TROPICS, PUNCH or Dawn).
  • Mishap Board: a reverse mode. Players are given a mission that was lost (drag, a dead orbit, radiation, a data bottleneck) and must find the design decision that caused it.

Why it matters

Students rarely get to experiment with a whole mission at once, so trade-offs stay abstract. Here, one decision visibly moves every other number: add a radar and the power, link and cost go red; choose a cheaper launcher and the mass margin disappears. Failing is safe and quick to repeat, and the Mishap Board turns failure into the lesson.

How it was built

HTML, CSS and plain JavaScript in a single page, hosted on GitHub Pages. Orbits, Δv, launch energy (C3), eclipse, revisit and link budgets use standard two-body and link equations, simplified from what NASA's GMAT computes at high fidelity. Instrument, launcher and mission figures are rounded public values; each instrument card names the real instrument it is modelled on, and the Help page lists every source. Costs, reliability and random events are our own simple models and are labelled as such. Deep Space Express (nuclear-pulse and antimatter drives) is speculative and labelled as speculative.

What we considered

Readable for students; honest about where numbers come from and which ones are estimates; keyboard, mouse and touch input; a hot-seat team mode on one screen so a classroom needs only one device.

Use of AI

The code was written with AI assistance (Anthropic Claude: Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Fable 5.2), directed, reviewed and tested by our team. The voice-over in the demo video was generated with an AI voice tool (Grok). No AI-generated images or video are used; the video is a screen recording of the game.

Prior work

Mission Design Lab was written during the hackathon (14–15 November 2026). Its colour palette and fonts were reused from an earlier personal project of the team owner.
